Key Research Thinking Patterns: Contrastive Learning: The researcher employs unsupervised contrastive learning to uncover structure in oral potentially malignant diseases, improving clustering performance and enabling clinicians to optimize patient treatment by understanding their risk level for developing oral cancer.

Tissue-Specific Fine-Tuning: The researcher proposes a tissue-specific fine-tuning approach to improve model performance and fairness in multispectral autofluorescence imaging for oral cancer diagnosis, increasing overall performance by 1.76% to 5.16% and decreasing the fairness gap by over 5%.

Multitask Learning: The researcher uses a multitask framework with margin delineation and cancer diagnosis tasks to improve automated in vivo oral cancer diagnosis from multispectral autofluorescence lifetime images, achieving a sensitivity of 82.08% and specificity of 75.92% on the cancer diagnosis task.

Pseudo Color Image Generation: The researcher investigates the impact of using morphological information in classifying suspicious breast lesions using pseudo color image generation, demonstrating that pseudo color sets containing the manually segmented mass performed significantly better than all other pseudo color sets.
Summary Description: Javier Jo is a researcher specializing in biomedical engineering, electrical and computer engineering, and cancer research. His primary focus is on developing machine learning-based methods for oral cancer diagnosis, risk stratification of oral lesions, and non-invasive cancer detection. He employs techniques such as unsupervised contrastive learning, multitask learning, and tissue-specific fine-tuning to improve model performance and fairness. His work involves the use of multispectral autofluorescence imaging, frequency domain imaging, and pseudo color image generation to enable clinicians to optimize patient treatment and improve early-stage cancer diagnosis.
